\chapter{Six to Ten, and the Character That Was Already Here}
\label{ch:zh-count-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say, hear, read and write the Mandarin numbers one to ten with their tones, and write the five characters this chapter adds.}

Five characters and twelve strokes finish a run the book abandoned at five seventeen chapters earlier -- with \zh{八} set against \zh{人}, and \zh{十} finally taught on its own after thirteen chapters inside \zh{早}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[liù]{\zh{六} — four strokes again, for six this time}

\label{lesson:ZH-W20-liu}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{五}. How many strokes, and how many does it mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — a dot, a bar, two legs}
\begin{quote}
\zh{六}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Four strokes. For six.} \zh{五} had four for five; \zh{六} has four for six. Whatever was left of the counting trick after chapter 3 is now gone for good.

The four strokes, in order:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the short \textbf{diǎn} dot at the top centre, down and to the right
  \item the long \textbf{héng} horizontal beneath it, left to right
  \item the left leg, a \textbf{piě} falling to the lower left
  \item the right leg, a \textbf{nà} falling to the lower right
\end{enumerate}

Top before bottom, then left before right — the two rules that have ordered every character in this book.

Hold on to strokes 3 and 4. On their own, without the dot and the bar, they are the character for \textbf{eight}, and you will write them again in two lessons.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{六} — dot, bar, left leg, right leg
  \item \emph{Cover:} write it again from memory
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%85\%AD.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{六}}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[liù]{\zh{六} — six, and the run starts again}

\label{lesson:ZH-C20-liu}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{六}, then count aloud to five.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{六}} \emph{liù} means \textbf{six}.

\textbf{liù} is \textbf{fourth tone} — the sharp fall, the same shape as \emph{sì}, four. Say them together and only the mouth changes: \textbf{sì, liù}.

The vowel is worth a moment. Pinyin writes \emph{iu}, and what you say is closer to \emph{ioū}: there is a faint \textbf{o} in the middle that the spelling does not print.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the run starts again}]
This book taught \zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} \zh{四} \zh{五} in chapter 3 and then stopped. For seventeen chapters it could name a family, a school and a greeting and could not count to six — could not give an age, a price, a floor or a date. \textbf{\zh{六}} is where that starts being paid back.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{sì}, \textbf{liù} — one fall, twice
  \item \textbf{yī èr sān sì wǔ liù} — the run, at speed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[qī]{\zh{七} — two strokes, for seven}

\label{lesson:ZH-W20-qi}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{六} and say how many strokes it has.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the second stroke does the work}
\begin{quote}
\zh{七}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Two strokes. For seven.} Six had four, seven has two — the stroke count is not merely useless now, it is running backwards.

The two strokes:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{héng} horizontal, left to right, rising a little as it goes
  \item the \textbf{shùwāngōu}: start high on the right, descend, bend along the foot to the right, and hook upward at the end
\end{enumerate}

That second stroke is one continuous movement with two turns in it. Do not lift in the middle of it — a lift is what makes it two strokes instead of one, and seven would then be three.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{七} — the bar, then the turning stroke, unbroken
  \item \emph{Count:} two strokes, not three
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E4\%B8\%83.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{七}}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[qī]{\zh{七} — seven}

\label{lesson:ZH-C20-qi}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{七}, then say six.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{七}} \emph{qī} means \textbf{seven}.

\textbf{qī} is \textbf{first tone}, the high level one — the same shape as \emph{yī}, one. Say them in a row and hold the pitch flat across both: \textbf{yī, qī}.

The \textbf{q} is the piece to work on, because English has no letter for it. Put the tongue where it goes for \textbf{y} in \emph{yes}, then release the air the way you do for \textbf{ch}. It is not the \emph{k} of \emph{queen} and it is not an English \emph{ch}; it is the tongue of one and the release of the other.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{yī}, \textbf{qī} — two high level tones
  \item \textbf{wǔ liù qī} — dip, fall, level
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bā]{\zh{八} — a character you have already written twice}

\label{lesson:ZH-W20-ba}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{七}, then write \zh{六} and put a finger on its two legs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the gap is the character}
\begin{quote}
\zh{八}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Two strokes. For eight.}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the left leg, a \textbf{piě} falling to the lower left
  \item lift, then the right leg, a \textbf{nà} falling to the lower right
\end{enumerate}

You wrote both of them in \zh{六} two lessons ago, under the dot and the bar. Take the dot and the bar away and what is left is eight.

And one more comparison, because it is the sharpest in the whole book: \textbf{\zh{人}}, \emph{rén}, \textquotedblleft{}person\textquotedblright{}, is these same two strokes \textbf{joined at the top}. \zh{八} is the same two strokes \textbf{parted}. The gap is the entire difference between a person and the number eight — which is why the first stroke of \zh{八} begins below where \zh{人}'s does, and why the two must never be allowed to touch.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{八} — left leg, lift, right leg, apart at the top
  \item \emph{Contrast:} write \zh{人} beside it and mark where they meet
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%85\%AB.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{八}}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bā]{\zh{八} — eight, and why it costs more}

\label{lesson:ZH-C20-ba}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{八}, then say seven.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{八}} \emph{bā} means \textbf{eight}.

\textbf{bā} is \textbf{first tone}, high and level, like \emph{qī}. The \textbf{b} is unaspirated: no puff of air, closer to an English \emph{p} in \emph{spin} than the \emph{b} of \emph{bin}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{bā} sounds close to \emph{fā}, the first syllable of a word meaning to prosper or come into wealth. That resemblance is why eight is the number people pay extra for: on a car number plate, in a phone number, in the price of a flat on the eighth floor. The Beijing Olympics opened at eight seconds past eight on the eighth day of the eighth month.

A number can carry that much only in a language where numbers sound like other words, and this is the clearest case of it a beginner will meet.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{qī}, \textbf{bā} — two level tones
  \item \textbf{liù qī bā} — fall, level, level
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jiǔ]{\zh{九} — two strokes again}

\label{lesson:ZH-W20-jiu}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{八} and \zh{七}. How many strokes between them? Say why eight is the number people pay extra for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — a fall and a turn}
\begin{quote}
\zh{九}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Two strokes. For nine.}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item a long \textbf{piě}, falling from the upper right all the way to the lower left
  \item lift, then the \textbf{héngzhéwāngōu}: cross the first stroke to the right, turn downward, and hook back to the left at the foot
\end{enumerate}

Seven, eight and nine are two strokes each. \textbf{The last three single digits are the three quickest characters in this book to write}, and the three largest numbers you have. Whatever intuition said that bigger numbers need more ink is finished.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{九} — the long fall, then the crossing turn with its hook
  \item \zh{七} \zh{八} \zh{九} in a row — six strokes for three numbers
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E4\%B9\%9D.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{九}}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jiǔ]{\zh{九} — nine}

\label{lesson:ZH-C20-jiu}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{九}, then say eight.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{九}} \emph{jiǔ} means \textbf{nine}.

\textbf{jiǔ} is \textbf{third tone}, the low dip — so it joins \emph{nǐ}, \emph{hǎo} and \emph{wǔ}. Say all four in a row and let the pitch stay low and creaky across every one.

The \textbf{j} is the unaspirated partner of the \textbf{q} in \emph{qī}: same tongue position, no puff of air. Say \textbf{qī jiǔ} and the only difference is the breath.

Keep the dip in mind. Two third tones in a row do not both dip — the first one lifts — and nine is about to give this book its first pair of them.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{nǐ hǎo wǔ jiǔ} — four dips
  \item \textbf{qī jiǔ} — the same tongue, one with breath and one without
  \item \textbf{qī bā jiǔ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shí]{\zh{十} — the character that was already here}

\label{lesson:ZH-W20-shi}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{早}, \emph{zǎo}, morning. Say what sits under the sun in it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — a bar and a post}
\begin{quote}
\zh{十}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Two strokes. For ten.}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{héng} horizontal, left to right
  \item lift, then the \textbf{shù} vertical, top to bottom, crossing it at the centre
\end{enumerate}

You have written this before. It is the lower half of \textbf{\zh{早}} — and the morning lesson said, in as many words, that on its own this piece is the character for ten, and then went on to something else. It has been sitting on the page for thirteen chapters waiting for a number to hang on.

Set it against \textbf{\zh{一}}, one: the same horizontal, with a post through it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{十} — bar first, then post
  \item \zh{早} and point at the \zh{十} inside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%8D\%81.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{十}}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shí]{\zh{十} — ten}

\label{lesson:ZH-C20-shi}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{十}, then say nine.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{十}} \emph{shí} means \textbf{ten}.

\textbf{shí} is \textbf{second tone}, the rise — the pitch starts in the middle and goes up, as if asking. It is the first number in the whole run of ten to use it.

The \textbf{sh} curls the tongue back, further than an English \emph{sh}. Keep the tip high and behind the ridge.

Say the whole run once: \textbf{yī èr sān sì wǔ liù qī bā jiǔ shí}. Level, fall, level, fall, dip, fall, level, level, dip, rise.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the last of the ten}]
Ten is not simply the tenth word. It is the last one this book needs before \textbf{every number up to ninety-nine falls out of the ten it already has} — and the next chapter spends it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{bā jiǔ shí} — level, dip, rise
  \item the whole run, one to ten, at speed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[Practice]{Payoff — one to ten}

\label{lesson:ZH-C20-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say ten, then say why eight costs more.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Count aloud one to ten, then ten to one.
  \item Hear all ten named singly and out of order, and say each.
  \item Read the ten characters printed shuffled — \zh{九} \zh{三} \zh{十} \zh{六} \zh{一} \zh{八} \zh{四} \zh{七} \zh{二} \zh{五} — and say each with its tone.
  \item Write the five new ones from dictation: \zh{六} \zh{七} \zh{八} \zh{九} \zh{十}.
  \item Say the tone of each of the ten in order. Only one of them rises.
  \item Say what \zh{八} and \zh{人} differ by, and what sits inside \zh{早}.
\end{enumerate}

Five new characters cost \textbf{twelve strokes between them} — four, two, two, two and two. The single hardest thing in this chapter was not the writing; it was that the numbers had been left at five for seventeen chapters.
